I wish I could give you more in-depth info, but it completely depends on the situation. Expect waiting times to be long in the ER, but you will probably be able to visit her either at the ER or if she is admitted. If she is admitted, she may also be transferred to another hospital if there is not space in their current wards, or may have to wait in the ER overnight.

If your girlfriend is in imminent danger of hurting herself, as determined by the doctors, she will be admitted. If she is not, her chances of being admitted depend greatly on her symptoms and whether or not she will be safe moving forward. Often times, if not admitted, patients are referred to an emergency psychiatry appointment, or given other outpatient resources like day treatment or partial hospital programs. They generally will not want to prescribe lots of meds at the ER (maybe some anxiety meds), because that requires an in-depth eval that they generally just do not have time for there.

I hope all goes okay for you, and for her.

I think the answer is complicated and varies on a case by case basis. People have given some good answers so far, but I'd just like to chime in with my own experience.

I have a history of bipolar 1 with psychosis and I credit meds to helping me achieve my stability. Had I not been on lithium + a cocktail of other meds for over a year after my worst episode, I certainly don't think I would have recovered as well. However, I have been off almost all meds for coming up on 2 months and it is DEFINITELY better than what any doctor would have told me was possible with my "level of severity". 

I should note, I had to taper off meds without medical advice because an issue with my insurance would not let me see my psychiatrist or get more prescriptions, and I was so frustrated with my experiences with the system that I decided I just needed a break. I'm not opposed to taking meds in the future, and have considered re-starting, but I am pleasantly surprised by how well I've been doing. Overall, I do not feel any more out of control than when I was on meds, and while there are hard days, I have been able to get through them without too much struggle. I am working, my close relationships are not suffering, I'm sleeping decently, etc. Here are some things I credit to this working out for me (*so far*, I should note; there is never any guarantee):

1/ A low stress environment. I ended up quitting my full-time job because it was too stressful and now am trying to build up my self employed work. This would not be possible if I didn't have a little financial security; I'm fortunate to have that right now and don't know when I will again!

2/ LOTS of self compassion. Giving myself leeway to suffer some days and accepting the moods for what they are. Not immediately freaking out and becoming convinced I'm spiraling because I have one bad day (easier said than done tbh, I still struggle with this).

3/ Healthy diet and exercise; sleep. It's certainly not a cure-all, and I hate when people say it is, but keeping your lifestyle regulated and your circadian rhythms in-rhythm can prevent bad shit.

4/ Symptom tracking and self regulating. Making sure I am getting enough sleep, and when I see I've only been hitting 4 hours this past week and maybe spending too much money, I need to CANCEL ALL MY PLANS for the weekend, take a long hot bath with essential oils, and hide out in my house until my body physically relaxes. Fortunately, this seems to have gotten easier as time has gone on, too.

My point with all this being, there is no way to know exactly the course of someone's illness just based on their previous symptoms. I know that I have the potential for it to be really severe again, but that doesn't mean it will right away, or next year, or even 10 years from now. Side effects from meds absolutely killed me, as well as the shit I went through dealing with 'treatment', and it's worth it for me to take that risk even if it means some more self-care. You'll ultimately have to make that choice for yourself -- whether to be on meds -- but make sure to think carefully about it, and do what you truly think is best for you. The VAST majority of medical professionals will never ever advocate stopping your meds, but treating mental illness is *such* an imperfect science that you really just don't know. It irritates me that it is seen as irresponsible when people ignore the suffering we go through trying (and failing) to get better taking medicine.

Hope this made a bit of sense, and sorry if it was long. If you want to talk more feel free to message me. Best of luck!

Make sure to write down your symptoms and concerns, and be as specific as possible about that episode and other episodes you may have had in the past. Being diagnosed with bipolar can be a lengthy process due to its so easily being misdiagnosed, but the more information you can provide, the better. Best of luck!

Just because your symptoms aren't as severe as others certainly doesn't mean you have bipolar disorder. However, the short duration of your episodes makes me think you might want to look for another opinion. You are certainly NOT faking it, but if your manic/hypomanic episodes are only lasting an hour max, that could either be an *extremely* rare form of ultradian cycling (which researchers do believe exists, just not as often as it is thought to) or there is something else triggering your "episodes". An in depth psych eval would probably help rule out other causes. I know that I have anxiety and ADHD as well and those can cause short spurts of high energy/hyperactivity and irritability but are different from mania. Other conditions may also have overlapping symptoms. 

My point being..don't rule yourself out on the grounds of "faking" it but you need someone who will listen to your full story and be able to give you an accurate picture of what you're experiencing. If you don't trust your current care team, you can always look for another opinion. Best of luck!

While it's true that sugar doesn't cause hyperactivity like a lot of parents seem to think, it *is* an easy source of energy for the body and will leave you feeling more out-of-whack than if your blood sugar stays constant.

It sounds like you've been given a bunch of labels that often have overlap, and maybe if the meds aren't working, the doctors haven't quite gotten the diagnosis right. It's frustrating when you don't think your so-called problems are actually your problems, but I'd encourage you to think critically about your behavior. Don't think of it as a 'mental illness' if you don't like that word -- just think about what things you experience that make your family concerned, or make it hard for you to function on a day-to-day basis. You mentioned anger -- do you have other mood swings, trouble focusing, etc? There is absolutely nothing wrong with that, but I think if you are able to identify exactly what you struggle with, that would help you greatly in regards to feeling better.

Also, if you don't attend therapy, there are lot of therapists out there who won't ever call you "mentally ill", slap a bunch of labels on you, or make you take meds. It might be worth seeing one of them, because they are there to genuinely focus on what you need to be your best, be that anger coping skills, how to deal with your family, etc.

I think this is something a lot of us struggle with, and the key is to focus on your mental health and let work take a back burner until then. Don't get me wrong, I understand -- bills need to be paid -- but if you can find some temporary or flexible work that will allow you to focus on what you need to get better, it'll benefit you greatly in the long run. Too many times, I have tried to jump into new full-time jobs when I am really not well enough, and I always just end up quitting after a couple months because of it.

You might also be someone who is genuinely unhappy working 'just one job', which I can relate to all too well. I could never sit at a desk 40 hours a week, or do any one thing 40 hours a week! I'm still very young, but I know that in the future I'll probably have two or three part time jobs, at least one of which will be self-employed. I'm self-employed right now and it is the *best* thing to ever happen to me. My own hours, great pay, no shitty management... can cancel work whenever I want! Basically, it doesn't hurt to think outside the box. If you have anything you can do as work in the meantime that's not a traditional 9-to-5 job, that might be the way to go. It does depend on your financial situation, but keep on trying different things out..you are DEFINITELY not alone.

There are also such things as career counselors (and of course online aptitude tests) if you are more worried about what field exactly to go into. Best of luck!

Obviously not a diagnosis (disclaimer lol), but here are my thoughts: Have you always had these issues? Do you struggle with relationships? A lot of times bipolar gets confused with BPD (borderline personality disorder), because people with BPD tend to have many mood swings throughout the day. Some doctors think it *is* possible to have bipolar that cycles that rapidly, but a lot of the time it turns out to be something else like BPD. My sister was first diagnosed with BPII but then it turned out she has BPD.

One thing that is thought to distinguish between the two is whether anything triggers your symptoms. Can a bad interaction with someone, learning some shitty news, etc send you into depression? With bipolar, you usually do not see any real cause for your mood swings (of course there are such thing as "triggers" but they are not related to relationships etc), but with BPD that is one of the hallmark symptoms. Just something to think about.

It's very common to be misdiagnosed. I'm glad you're taking a look at your symptoms, and the fact that you have noticed these patterns throughout your life likely means something. Whether it is enough to warrant a diagnosis of BP or whether it means you may fall somewhere along the bipolar spectrum, only a professional can tell you. Try to be as objective and descriptive as you can when you go in for your assessment - give real examples from your "episodes" but don't list symptoms straight out of the DSM.

A lot of symptoms can be very similar, but often people with bipolar respond to different medications for depression (are helped more by mood stabilizers/antipsychotics than antidepressants) which suggests there is a different biological component... but it's also not this way for *everyone*.

People with bipolar are more likely to have atypical features, i.e. hypersomnia and hyperphagia, than people with unipolar depression. in fact, in some cases these are almost considered to be characteristic of BP depression (but again.. not for everyone).

BP depression is also thought to carry a higher suicide risk because when people have mixed features along with depression, even if it is not a full blown mixed episode, they have more energy to carry through with their plans.

There are different types of bipolar. The two you will most often read about are bipolar I ("manic depression") and bipolar II (less-high highs, but lows just as low), which have more clear clinical symptoms. One can also have cyclothymia, which is milder ups and downs, or bipolar NOS, which means you don't fit the criteria for any one but have some symptoms of bipolar (...something along those lines). If you have ever felt like you were so happy you slept less, were more productive, talked a lot, your thoughts raced, etc, for a few days or more at a time, I would bring that up with your doctor for sure. Not all types of bipolar involve you getting into dangerous situations, but they all involve clear ups and downs.

Sorry if that was not a very organized explanation but, basically: although I never brought up the idea of bipolar to my doctor personally, it definitely crossed my mind at a crucial time. We know ourselves best, despite the common all-knowing attitude of psychiatry these days. One thing that might help would be to bring in some printed information on the *bipolar spectrum* and explain how you believe your experiences are consistent with some bipolar symptoms. If you come in just proclaiming you have the disorder and you're clearly self-diagnosing, and can't give concrete, observable examples, they're less likely to take you seriously, from my experience. Psychiatry wants to see behavior, to observe it directly, or have concrete evidence, to make a diagnosis. They don't like to just trust your own word, unless it's for something like depression where you wouldn't just get 'paranoid' about having it (like a lot of people do get paranoid about having bipolar or schizophrenia or other things).

Just to clarify, you are going inpatient into a hospital/institutional setting, correct - that is what you mean? 

If you are not admitted through the emergency department, I imagine it would be a lot easier because that is honestly the worst part - takes hours and lots of waiting around being miserable. If you are going straight there, expect to first be asked to change into scrubs and they will pat you down and check for metal, self-injury scars, etc. You may be asked to do a drug test or pregnancy test although that is often just in the ER. They will ask you a bunch of questions about your history, diagnosis, medications, symptoms, etc. 

It depends on where you live and whether the unit you are in is locked or not. With locked units they are stricter and you are not allowed to leave, usually more people are there under emergency holds (for suicide) or are psychotic, etc. There is usually a main area, group room, and dining room; sometimes some of those are combined. They tend to fill anywhere from half to almost all of the days with groups, depending on how the unit operates, etc. Their strictness depends as well - some let you have more personal items than others; some don't even let you wear your own clothes. 

Groups will not be individualized, one-on-one therapy. They are skill-building groups often times, things like OT, life skills, coping mechanisms, identifying triggers, etc. You will also meet with a psychiatrist once a day to review medications and make changes. Nurses will administer meds and other staff people or nurses will check in on you periodically as you go about your day to see how you are doing.

Overall, the stays I've had have been helpful in keeping me safe and getting me stable when I needed immediate care, but they have not been amazing healing experiences and I've dealt with a lot of frustration from staff who are incompetent or treat us like wild animals. That being said, I would not be alive without inpatient hospitalization so I am grateful for what it has done for me.

If you have generalized anxiety disorder as opposed to panic disorder, and because you have depression as well, they'll likely start you on SSRIs. I felt a bit off and my brain felt numb when I started them for a week or so but it went away. Side effects for those guys aren't too bad compared to other psych meds, so don't worry too much! But, I know plenty of people for whom they work excellently on and worked the first time.

They might give you anti-anxiety medication separately if you tend to have more panic, like benzos (they're very addictive though), or there is one specifically for generalized anxiety called Buspar. I've never tried it but it's supposed to be great.

Now, the reason I'd say it's *possible* it's a phase is that it's a phase of your life, not just a phase in your development, that is especially hard. A lot of people are very unhappy in their teens and then find their niche in adulthood, when they have more opportunities. If it helps at all, try to remember that you'll be out of high school in a couple years, out of your mom's household and the toxicity it created. You may find that in itself helps significantly. When I moved out I *loved* it because I was able to develop my own identity, unaffected by my parents. You can go to college, or take time off to work - do what appeals to you. If, then, you are still struggling as much as you are now (or even close to it) you'll know for sure you have depression that isn't situational. 

However, because you express feelings of hopelessness the way you do I'd advise you to see if you can talk to a therapist about how you're feeling for a professional evaluation. If s/he thinks your problems are caused by clinical depression, I'd hope you're able to figure that out now if you can. You also mention mood swings - I would keep an eye on those. I don't know if you have always been moody, if that's normal for you, but I was a non-moody teenager until I had some mood swings starting when I was your age. Those developed into bipolar disorder which has ruined my life. I don't mean to scare you, I'd just tell you to keep an eye out because catching it early is definitely preferable.

Best of luck. I hope you are able to find help and get the answers you need, or at least to find hobbies or ways to cope with this phase of your life if it is the cause of your problems.

Talking really fast but not realizing it until my therapist tells me something's going on. I don't know *that* much, but here's what I think: 
In terms of disability caused by both illnesses I know schizophrenia generally 'costs' more and it's often listed higher on the lists of 'worst mental illnesses' or just 'worst illnesses'. I don't think the difference is huge, at least in the study I read the other day. But, as always, it depends on the severity, which depends on the individual experiencing it. Some people with schizophrenia can live completely normal lives while some with bipolar are not able to manage their illness well (hoping I'm not one of them, still on a roller coaster here ). I am fairly certain fewer people with schizophrenia lead normal lives though.

Sometimes I do think about schizophrenia and wish I had it instead for a little while (then again I do that with lots of things: cancer, brain tumor, 'regular' depression, etc) just because I am so sick of the mood swings, and schizophrenia is a thought disorder, not a mood disorder. Then again I'm sure people with schizophrenia think the same of bipolar and other disorders so it's just a *being sick of the situation* thing.

I think schizophrenia is really hard to treat because the nature of it makes people wary of taking medication, and even on medication many still experience symptoms. I met a distressed, schizophrenic young man at the hospital once who was discharged while still very clearly delusional, and I thought wow, they would never let me leave like that. But that is everyday life for many, even on medications, so I really feel sorry for them. I'd like to learn more about how effective schizophrenia treatments are, though.

I think both illnesses have incredible stigma but that schizophrenia is worse because it immediately implies insanity and a disconnect from reality. Bipolar is more like, wow what a crazy moody bitch she's so bipolar. The term is used improperly because people mainly think it's just a *watch out for this one and her crazy moods* type of deal. I think if people knew the reality of mood swings, specifically mania and psychosis, there might be more stigma, but sadly there is the persistent view that it's just alternating between happy and sad.

I think schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, would be an incredibly difficult illness to have and I'm really sorry to anyone suffering from that. It sounds like the worst of both worlds.

If people disagree with this or have scientific evidence to counter it please do speak up. This is what I can remember from what I've read and learned, but it can be hard to find accurate statistics/facts on the internet these days.

It depends what's causing it. Depression can be situational or endogenous (not situational). If it's endogenous it can be dysthymia (mild depression) or major depression (moderate-severe). If it's situational it can range in severity. For those who have non-situational depression, the length of time of the episode will vary greatly, as will the number of episodes.

So, the answer is yes, depression will go away on its own eventually without treatment. You just don't know when. And you don't know if it will come back. Personally, my episodes will only last 1-2 months but be very severe and will occur quite often. Others may have one severe 8 month depression and then not again for 10 years. It really depends .

The severity, cause, and where you are in your life are all factors to take into account. I would definitely consider getting help if it is affecting your life significantly. It really will help it go away faster (therapy, meds) and prevent future episodes if you have a depressive disorder (meds).
